summary: How the kidney handles glucose, protein, calcium, phosphate, potassium, and toxic alcohols, and how it makes erythropoietin and active vitamin D. Exam cases hand you a lab panel and ask you to predict the next value or name the step that went wrong.

notes.h: Glucose reabsorption and the renal threshold
points: All filtered glucose is normally reabsorbed in the proximal tubule by sodium-coupled transport.
SGLT2 in the early proximal tubule takes up about 90 percent; SGLT1 further along takes the rest. GLUT2 moves glucose out the basolateral side.
The carriers saturate. Glucose starts to spill into urine at a plasma level of about 200 mg/dL (renal threshold); all nephrons are saturated at the transport maximum (about 375 mg/min).
Glucose left in the tubule holds water with it (osmotic diuresis): polyuria, thirst, and volume depletion in uncontrolled diabetes.
Glucosuria with normal plasma glucose points to a proximal tubule defect (Fanconi syndrome) or a lower threshold in pregnancy.
Glomerular: a damaged filter leaks albumin; can exceed 3.5 g/day (nephrotic). The dipstick detects albumin well.
Overflow: a normal filter is overwhelmed by small proteins made in excess, such as Bence Jones light chains in multiple myeloma.
Tubular: small proteins (beta-2 microglobulin, light chains) are filtered normally but the proximal tubule fails to reclaim them; usually under 2 g/day.
The dipstick misses most light chains and tubular proteins; urine protein electrophoresis or immunofixation finds them.

notes.h: Calcium, phosphate, vitamin D, and magnesium
points: Liver adds the 25-hydroxyl; the proximal tubule adds the 1-alpha-hydroxyl to make calcitriol, the active form.
1-alpha-hydroxylase is turned up by PTH and low phosphate and turned down by FGF23 and high phosphate.
Calcitriol raises gut absorption of calcium and phosphate.
Low magnesium blocks PTH release and causes PTH resistance, so hypocalcemia will not correct until magnesium is replaced.
Into cells (lowers serum K): insulin and beta-2 stimulation (both turn up Na/K-ATPase) and alkalosis.
Out of cells (raises serum K): acidosis, cell lysis (rhabdomyolysis, tumor lysis, hemolysis), insulin deficiency, and hyperosmolality (water leaves cells and drags K with it).
Hyperkalemia ECG: peaked T waves, then PR prolongation and loss of P waves, a wide QRS, a sine wave, and ventricular fibrillation.
Hypokalemia ECG: flat T waves, ST depression, and U waves; muscle weakness and arrhythmias.
Made by peritubular interstitial (fibroblast-like) cells of the renal cortex and outer medulla when they sense low oxygen delivery.
Hypoxia stabilizes HIF, which switches on the EPO gene; EPO keeps red cell precursors alive in the marrow.
Chronic kidney disease: lost EPO-producing tissue gives a normocytic, normochromic anemia.
Renal cell carcinoma can make EPO on its own, giving secondary polycythemia with a high EPO level.
Alcohol dehydrogenase (using NAD+) starts the breakdown: ethylene glycol to glycolaldehyde, then glycolic acid, glyoxylic acid, and oxalic acid.
Early: the intact alcohol raises the osmolal gap. Later: the acids give a high anion gap metabolic acidosis as the osmolal gap falls.
Oxalate binds calcium: hypocalcemia, calcium oxalate crystals in urine, and acute tubular injury.
Blocking alcohol dehydrogenase (fomepizole, or ethanol as a competing substrate) stops toxic acids from forming.
Nephrotic syndrome: the liver makes more lipoproteins in response to low oncotic pressure, and lipoprotein breakdown slows, so cholesterol and LDL rise.
Lipiduria shows as oval fat bodies and fatty casts; their cholesterol esters give a Maltese cross under polarized light.

tricks.label: Gap swap
tricks.text: In ethylene glycol poisoning the osmolal gap comes first and the anion gap comes later, because the parent alcohol is turned into acids over hours.

tricks.label: Insulin and beta push K in
tricks.text: Both turn up the Na/K-ATPase. Anything that breaks cells or adds acid pushes K out.

tricks.label: Fix magnesium first
tricks.text: Calcium that will not come up despite replacement means check magnesium; without it the parathyroid cannot release PTH and tissues ignore what PTH there is.

highYield: Glucosuria begins at a plasma glucose of about 200 mg/dL.
CKD: high phosphate, low calcitriol, low or normal calcium, high PTH.
Primary hyperparathyroidism: high calcium, low phosphate.
Peaked T waves are the first ECG sign of hyperkalemia; U waves mark hypokalemia.
Anemia of CKD is normocytic from low EPO; renal cell carcinoma can cause polycythemia from excess EPO.
Ethylene glycol: high anion gap acidosis, osmolal gap, calcium oxalate crystals, acute kidney injury.
Maltese crosses in urine mean lipiduria from nephrotic syndrome.
pitfalls: A negative dipstick does not rule out light chain proteinuria; the dipstick reacts mainly with albumin.
Hemolyzed blood samples give false hyperkalemia; repeat the draw before acting on an isolated high K.
Vitamin D deficiency and CKD both raise PTH, but phosphate is low in vitamin D deficiency and high in CKD.
Isopropanol raises the osmolal gap without an anion gap acidosis; ethylene glycol and methanol give both.

summary: The single-gene and tumor suppressor disorders that show up in the kidney: polycystic kidney disease, type IV collagen disease, VHL, WT1, tuberous sclerosis, cystinuria, and Fabry disease. Questions ask you to name the gene or protein, read the inheritance in a pedigree, and link the defect to the kidney finding.

points: Autosomal dominant (ADPKD): PKD1 on chromosome 16 (polycystin-1, about 85 percent, more severe) or PKD2 on chromosome 4 (polycystin-2, milder).
Polycystins sit on the primary cilium and control calcium signaling; loss raises cAMP and drives cell growth and fluid secretion into cysts.
ADPKD: both kidneys large and full of cysts in adults, flank pain, hematuria, hypertension, liver cysts, berry aneurysms, mitral valve prolapse.
Autosomal recessive (ARPKD): PKHD1 on chromosome 6 (fibrocystin) causes cysts in infants, oligohydramnios with Potter sequence, and congenital hepatic fibrosis.
Dominant pedigree: every generation, both sexes, father to son passing, each child of an affected parent has a 50 percent risk. Recessive: unaffected carrier parents, each child has a 1 in 4 risk.
The glomerular basement membrane uses a network of alpha-3, alpha-4, and alpha-5 chains of type IV collagen.
Alport syndrome: most often X-linked COL4A5 mutation; less often autosomal recessive COL4A3 or COL4A4.
Alport triad: hematuria progressing to kidney failure, sensorineural hearing loss, and eye defects (anterior lenticonus).
Electron microscopy in Alport: a split, layered basket-weave basement membrane with areas of thinning and thickening.
Thin basement membrane disease: heterozygous COL4A3 or COL4A4 mutation, a uniformly thin membrane, persistent microscopic hematuria, usually normal kidney function.
VHL is a tumor suppressor on chromosome 3p. Its protein tags HIF for destruction when oxygen is normal.
Loss of both copies stabilizes HIF, which drives VEGF (new vessels), PDGF, and EPO, so clear cell tumors are very vascular.
Sporadic clear cell carcinoma: both hits are somatic (often 3p deletion plus mutation of the other copy), one tumor in an older adult.
VHL syndrome (autosomal dominant): one germline hit, so tumors are early, bilateral, and multiple, with cerebellar and retinal hemangioblastomas and pheochromocytoma.
WT1 on 11p13 codes a transcription factor needed for kidney and gonad development.
WAGR (11p13 deletion): Wilms tumor, aniridia (PAX6), genitourinary anomalies, and intellectual disability.
Denys-Drash: WT1 point mutation with early diffuse mesangial sclerosis, nephrotic syndrome, and 46,XY disorder of sex development.
Beckwith-Wiedemann: 11p15 imprinting defect (extra IGF2 expression) with macroglossia, organomegaly, hemihyperplasia, omphalocele, and neonatal hypoglycemia.
Tuberous sclerosis (autosomal dominant): TSC1 (hamartin, chromosome 9) or TSC2 (tuberin, chromosome 16) normally brakes mTOR; loss lets mTOR drive cell growth.
Kidney in tuberous sclerosis: angiomyolipomas (blood vessels, smooth muscle, fat), often multiple and bilateral and prone to bleeding, plus renal cysts.
Cystinuria (autosomal recessive): faulty proximal tubule and gut transporter for cystine, ornithine, lysine, and arginine (COLA).
Cystine dissolves poorly in acidic urine, so it forms hexagonal crystals and stones; the cyanide-nitroprusside test turns red-purple.
Fabry disease (X-linked recessive): alpha-galactosidase A deficiency builds up globotriaosylceramide in vessels, nerves, sweat glands, and kidney.
Fabry signs: angiokeratomas, burning pain in hands and feet, little sweating, corneal whorls, proteinuria leading to kidney failure, and heart and stroke disease.

Goodpasture antibodies target the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen; Alport patients lack normal alpha-3, 4, 5 networks.
VHL loss keeps HIF active, which drives VEGF and EPO in clear cell carcinoma.
TSC2 lies next to PKD1 on chromosome 16, so a deletion of both gives severe early polycystic disease.
Fabry disease and Hunter syndrome are the classic X-linked lysosomal storage diseases.
pitfalls: Cystinuria (transporter defect, stones) differs from cystinosis (lysosomal cystine buildup, Fanconi syndrome).
Alport and thin basement membrane disease both cause hematuria; only Alport brings hearing loss and progressive kidney failure.
WAGR and Beckwith-Wiedemann both raise Wilms risk but at different 11p sites: 11p13 (WT1) versus 11p15 (imprinting).
Angiomyolipoma contains fat; renal cell carcinoma rarely does, which helps on imaging.

summary: How antibodies, immune complexes, ANCA, and T cells injure the kidney, how complement levels sort glomerular disease, and how the urinary tract keeps bacteria out. Exams also ask about immune attack on renal cell carcinoma and hepatitis B vaccine serology.

notes.h: Three immune patterns in the glomerulus
points: Type II (anti-GBM): IgG against the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen lays down in a smooth linear line along the GBM.
Goodpasture syndrome: the same antibody hits alveolar basement membrane, giving lung hemorrhage plus glomerulonephritis.
Type III (immune complex): complexes deposit or form in place, giving a granular, lumpy pattern. Examples: poststreptococcal GN, lupus nephritis, IgA nephropathy, membranous nephropathy.
Pauci-immune: little or no immunoglobulin on immunofluorescence; ANCA activate neutrophils that damage vessel walls. Examples: granulomatosis with polyangiitis, microscopic polyangiitis.
Low C3 with usually normal C4: poststreptococcal GN (alternative pathway) and membranoproliferative GN (C4 can also fall in the immune complex type).
Low C3 and C4: lupus nephritis (classical pathway); C4 is also low in cryoglobulinemia.
Normal complement: IgA nephropathy, anti-GBM disease, ANCA vasculitis.
Poststreptococcal C3 returns to normal in about 8 weeks; a C3 that stays low suggests membranoproliferative GN.
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis: PR3-ANCA (c-ANCA), necrotizing granulomas in sinuses, nose, and lungs, plus crescentic GN.
Microscopic polyangiitis: MPO-ANCA (p-ANCA), lung capillaritis and GN, no granulomas, spares the upper airway.
Polyarteritis nodosa: medium arteries, ANCA negative, spares glomeruli and lungs; renal artery microaneurysms cause infarcts and renin-driven hypertension; linked to hepatitis B.
IgA vasculitis in children: IgA complexes after an upper respiratory infection cause palpable purpura on buttocks and legs, arthralgia, abdominal pain, and intussusception.
IgA vasculitis kidney lesion: mesangial IgA deposits, the same as IgA nephropathy; platelets are normal.
One-way urine flow and complete bladder emptying wash bacteria out.
The ureter runs obliquely through the bladder wall, so a filling bladder squeezes it shut (flap valve) and stops reflux.
Infected urothelial cells shed into urine; uromodulin (Tamm-Horsfall protein) binds E. coli type 1 fimbriae.
Obstruction (stones, prostate enlargement, valves) causes stasis; vesicoureteral reflux carries bladder urine to the kidney.
Catheters bypass the urethra and carry biofilm; pregnancy relaxes and compresses the ureters, so bacteriuria often becomes pyelonephritis.

notes.h: Tumor immunity and the hepatitis B vaccine
points: CD8 T cells recognize renal cell carcinoma peptides on MHC class I and kill with perforin and granzymes.
NK cells kill cells that lose MHC class I (missing self) and carry stress ligands.
Tumors escape by losing MHC class I and by expressing PD-L1, which binds PD-1 on T cells and shuts them down.
The recombinant hepatitis B surface antigen vaccine induces T cell-dependent IgG anti-HBs.
Anti-HBs alone (anti-HBc negative) means vaccine immunity; anti-HBs with anti-HBc means a past infection that resolved.
Preventing hepatitis B prevents its membranous nephropathy, which comes from viral antigen immune complexes.

tricks.label: Linear, lumpy, or little
tricks.text: Linear IgG is anti-GBM, lumpy granular deposits are immune complexes, and little or no staining is pauci-immune ANCA disease.

tricks.label: Vaccine shows S only
tricks.text: The vaccine contains surface antigen only, so a vaccinated person makes anti-HBs and never anti-HBc.

tricks.text: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is PR3 and cytoplasmic staining; microscopic polyangiitis is MPO and perinuclear staining.

Low C3 and C4 together point to lupus nephritis.
IgA nephropathy, anti-GBM disease, and ANCA vasculitis keep normal complement.

Polyarteritis nodosa spares glomeruli and causes renal artery microaneurysms.
Palpable purpura on the buttocks and legs of a child after a cold is IgA vasculitis.
PD-L1 on tumor cells turns off PD-1 bearing T cells.
pitfalls: IgA nephropathy and IgA vasculitis share the same kidney lesion; the vasculitis adds skin, joint, and gut involvement.
Microscopic polyangiitis looks like granulomatosis with polyangiitis in the lung and kidney but has no granulomas and no upper airway disease.
A cell that loses MHC class I escapes CD8 T cells but becomes a target for NK cells.
Anti-HBs is protective, while anti-HBc shows real exposure to the virus.

summary: The bacteria, parasites, and viruses behind urinary tract infection, urethritis, stones, and infection-linked glomerular disease. Questions test virulence factors, lab identification, how to read a urinalysis, and which infection leads to which kidney lesion.

points: Uropathogenic E. coli: gram-negative, lactose-fermenting rod from the patient's own fecal flora; causes most community cystitis (roughly 75 to 95 percent).
Type 1 fimbriae bind mannose on bladder urothelium and cause cystitis; P fimbriae bind P blood group antigens on upper tract cells and cause pyelonephritis.
Staphylococcus saprophyticus: gram-positive coagulase-negative coccus, novobiocin resistant, second most common cause in young sexually active women.
Klebsiella: gram-negative lactose fermenter with a thick polysaccharide capsule that makes mucoid colonies.
Enterococcus: gram-positive cocci in pairs and chains, hardy in bile and salt, common after instrumentation.
Pseudomonas aeruginosa: oxidase-positive, non-lactose-fermenting gram-negative rod that forms biofilm on catheters.
Proteus mirabilis urease splits urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide.
Ammonia raises urine pH, and magnesium ammonium phosphate (struvite) precipitates.
Struvite grows into staghorn calculi that fill the renal pelvis and calyces and shelter bacteria.
Proteus swarms across blood agar in waves, a clue to its identity in the lab.
Leukocyte esterase comes from neutrophils and marks pyuria.
Nitrite forms when Enterobacterales reduce dietary nitrate; gram-positive organisms such as Enterococcus and S. saprophyticus leave it negative.
WBC casts form inside tubules, so they place the infection in the kidney (pyelonephritis).
Sterile pyuria (white cells but a negative routine culture): think urethritis from chlamydia or gonorrhea, or renal tuberculosis.
Neisseria gonorrhoeae: gram-negative diplococci, often inside neutrophils; pili attach to mucosa and change antigens, so immunity does not last.
Gonococcal IgA protease cleaves mucosal IgA; infection gives purulent discharge a few days after exposure.
Chlamydia trachomatis serovars D to K: obligate intracellular; the infectious elementary body enters the cell and becomes a reticulate body that divides inside an inclusion.
Chlamydia often causes scant discharge or none, and it is invisible on Gram stain.
Nucleic acid amplification testing of first-catch urine or a swab diagnoses both organisms.
Nephritogenic group A streptococci: poststreptococcal GN about 1 to 3 weeks after pharyngitis or 3 to 6 weeks after impetigo.
Hepatitis B: membranous nephropathy (also polyarteritis nodosa).
Hepatitis C: membranoproliferative GN with mixed cryoglobulinemia and low complement.
HIV: collapsing focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (HIV-associated nephropathy) with heavy proteinuria.
Renal tuberculosis spreads through the blood from the lung and forms caseating granulomas; urine shows sterile pyuria on routine culture.
Schistosoma haematobium: freshwater snails release cercariae that penetrate skin.
Adult worms live in the venules around the bladder; eggs with a terminal spine cross the bladder wall into urine.
Egg granulomas cause hematuria and fibrosis and raise the risk of squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder.

summary: Glomerulonephritis, glomerulosclerosis, nephrotic syndromes, and acute and chronic renal failure. Cases describe the urine, the biopsy, and the labs; you sort nephritic from nephrotic, name the lesion, and predict the complications.

points: Nephritic: inflammation tears capillary walls, giving hematuria with dysmorphic RBCs and RBC casts, oliguria, azotemia, hypertension, and proteinuria under 3.5 g/day.
Nephrotic: podocyte or membrane damage lets protein through, giving proteinuria over 3.5 g/day, low albumin, edema, hyperlipidemia, and fatty casts.

Nephrotic complications: edema from low oncotic pressure, high lipids from more hepatic lipoprotein synthesis, clots from urinary antithrombin III loss (renal vein thrombosis), infections from immunoglobulin loss.
Poststreptococcal GN: weeks after strep throat or impetigo; cola urine, periorbital edema, hypertension, low C3, granular IgG and C3, subepithelial humps on EM.
IgA nephropathy: gross hematuria within a day or two of a mucosal infection, mesangial IgA, normal C3; the most common GN worldwide.
Rapidly progressive GN: crescents of fibrin, parietal epithelial cells, and macrophages in most glomeruli, with kidney failure over weeks.
Crescentic types by immunofluorescence: linear (anti-GBM), granular (immune complex), little or none (pauci-immune, ANCA).
Lupus nephritis: diffuse proliferative class is most common and most severe, with subendothelial wire-loop deposits and a nephritic picture; membranous class gives nephrotic syndrome.
Lupus labs: low C3 and C4 and anti-dsDNA antibodies, which track nephritis activity.

Membranoproliferative GN: mesangial cells grow into the capillary wall and split the GBM (tram-track); immune complex type links to hepatitis B and C; dense deposit disease links to C3 nephritic factor.
Minimal change disease: children; selective albuminuria; normal light microscopy and immunofluorescence; foot process effacement on EM; excellent steroid response; linked to Hodgkin lymphoma.
Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis: scarring in parts of some glomeruli from podocyte injury, poor steroid response; secondary to HIV, heroin, sickle cell disease, and obesity.
Collapsing FSGS (HIV-associated nephropathy) collapses the capillary tuft and progresses fastest.
Membranous nephropathy: adults; subepithelial deposits with spike and dome GBM; anti-PLA2R antibodies in primary disease.
Secondary membranous causes: lupus, hepatitis B, solid tumors, and drugs such as NSAIDs; it carries the highest renal vein thrombosis risk.
Amyloidosis: AL (light chains) or AA (chronic inflammation) deposits in the glomerulus; Congo red shows apple-green birefringence under polarized light.
Early hyperfiltration raises GFR and strains the glomerulus.
Nonenzymatic glycation stiffens and thickens the basement membrane; hyaline arteriolosclerosis hits both afferent and efferent arterioles.
Mesangial matrix expands, first diffusely, then as nodules (Kimmelstiel-Wilson).
Course: microalbuminuria (30 to 300 mg/day), then overt proteinuria, nephrotic range, and kidney failure.
Prerenal (low perfusion): BUN to creatinine over 20, FENa under 1 percent, urine osmolality over 500 mOsm/kg; tubules work and hold sodium.
Intrinsic (acute tubular necrosis): BUN to creatinine under 15, FENa over 2 percent, urine osmolality under 350 mOsm/kg; tubules cannot hold sodium or concentrate.
Postrenal (obstruction): early values can look prerenal; with time they look like tubular injury.
Diabetes and hypertension are the two leading causes.
Uremia: fibrinous pericarditis, encephalopathy with asterixis, nausea, and platelet dysfunction with bleeding.
Also hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, volume overload with hypertension, normocytic anemia from low EPO, and renal osteodystrophy.
Waxy casts mark advanced chronic disease; kidneys are usually small and scarred.

tricks.label: MAD HUNGER
tricks.text: Consequences of kidney failure: Metabolic Acidosis, Dyslipidemia, Hyperkalemia, Uremia, Na and water retention, Growth delay, Erythropoietin failure, Renal osteodystrophy.

tricks.label: Days versus weeks
tricks.text: Hematuria within days of a sore throat is IgA nephropathy; hematuria weeks later with low C3 is poststreptococcal GN.

tricks.label: Where the deposit sits
tricks.text: Subepithelial (outside the GBM): poststreptococcal humps and membranous spikes. Subendothelial (inside): lupus wire loops and immune complex MPGN.

highYield: Over 3.5 g/day of protein defines nephrotic range.
Minimal change disease is the top cause of nephrotic syndrome in children; it responds to steroids.
Membranous nephropathy with anti-PLA2R is primary; look for lupus, hepatitis B, tumors, and NSAIDs if PLA2R is negative.
Renal vein thrombosis follows antithrombin III loss, most often in membranous nephropathy.
Crescents mean rapidly progressive GN; immunofluorescence tells which type.
Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules and efferent arteriole hyalinosis are signs of diabetic nephropathy.
FENa under 1 percent means the tubules still hold sodium (prerenal).
Uremic bleeding comes from platelet dysfunction with a normal platelet count.
pitfalls: IgA nephropathy and poststreptococcal GN both follow infections; timing and C3 tell them apart.
Membranous nephropathy and lupus class V share subepithelial deposits; check ANA and anti-dsDNA.
FSGS and minimal change both show effacement on EM; FSGS has scars on light microscopy and resists steroids.
Diuretics raise FENa, so a prerenal patient on diuretics can look intrinsic.
Diabetic nephropathy and amyloidosis keep kidneys normal size or large, unlike most chronic kidney disease.

summary: Acute tubular necrosis, the most common cause of intrinsic acute kidney injury, and Fanconi syndrome, a global failure of the proximal tubule. Questions ask for the cause, the cast, the phase of injury, and the lab pattern.

points: Ischemic: shock, sepsis, or long prerenal states starve tubular cells of oxygen.
Nephrotoxic: drugs, pigments, and poisons directly injure tubular cells.
Most vulnerable: the straight proximal tubule and the medullary thick ascending limb, which use a lot of ATP in low-oxygen areas.
Dead cells slough into the lumen and form casts that block flow and raise tubular pressure, lowering GFR.
Filtrate leaks back through the damaged wall, and afferent arteriole constriction lowers filtration further.
Urine: muddy brown granular casts and renal tubular epithelial cells; FENa over 2 percent.
Initiation (about 36 hours): the insult; urine output starts to fall.
Maintenance (1 to 3 weeks): oliguria, rising BUN and creatinine, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, and volume overload; hyperkalemia is the main danger.
Recovery: tubular cells regrow before they can concentrate urine, so polyuria washes out water, sodium, and potassium (risk of hypokalemia and dehydration).
Myoglobin from rhabdomyolysis (crush injury, extreme exertion, seizures); hemoglobin from intravascular hemolysis.
Aminoglycosides build up in proximal tubule cells; injury usually appears after about a week of therapy and is often nonoliguric.
Iodinated contrast constricts renal vessels and injures tubules, worst in diabetes and existing kidney disease.
Cisplatin injures the proximal tubule and wastes magnesium; ethylene glycol leaves calcium oxalate crystals.
Rhabdomyolysis: dipstick positive for blood (heme) but few or no RBCs on microscopy, very high CK, high potassium and phosphate, low calcium early.
Generalized proximal tubule failure: every proximal transporter leaks.
Glucosuria with normal plasma glucose, aminoaciduria, phosphaturia, and bicarbonaturia.
Bicarbonate loss gives proximal (type 2) renal tubular acidosis, a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis.
Phosphate loss causes rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults; potassium and uric acid are also lost.
Causes: cystinosis (most common inherited cause in children), Wilson disease, multiple myeloma light chains, heavy metals such as lead, and drugs such as tenofovir and ifosfamide.

tricks.label: Blood without blood
tricks.text: A dipstick that reads heme while the microscope shows no red cells means myoglobin or free hemoglobin.

tricks.label: Recovery drains
tricks.text: In the recovery phase the filter returns before the tubules can concentrate, so expect polyuria with low potassium.

tricks.label: Fanconi leaks everything small
tricks.text: Glucose, amino acids, phosphate, bicarbonate, uric acid, and potassium all spill because the whole proximal tubule fails.

highYield: Muddy brown granular casts mean acute tubular necrosis.
The straight proximal tubule and thick ascending limb are the most ischemia-sensitive segments.
Death in the oliguric phase usually comes from hyperkalemia.
Rhabdomyolysis: dipstick positive for blood, no RBCs, very high CK.
Aminoglycoside injury is often nonoliguric.
Fanconi syndrome: glucosuria with normal plasma glucose plus a normal anion gap acidosis.
Cystinosis is the classic inherited cause of Fanconi syndrome in children.
pitfalls: Prerenal injury has FENa under 1 percent and bland urine; tubular necrosis has FENa over 2 percent and granular casts.
Myoglobinuria leaves plasma clear; hemoglobinuria turns plasma pink.
Fanconi glucosuria occurs with normal plasma glucose; diabetic glucosuria needs plasma glucose above about 200 mg/dL.
Hyperkalemia belongs to the maintenance phase; hypokalemia belongs to recovery.

summary: Urinary obstruction and kidney stones: what blocks the flow at each age, what back pressure does to the kidney, and how stone type follows urine chemistry. Questions pair a patient with a likely cause, stone composition, or complication.

points: Newborn boys: posterior urethral valves block the bladder outlet and back up both kidneys.
Infants and children: ureteropelvic junction obstruction, the most common cause of congenital hydronephrosis.
Young adults: stones.
Pregnancy: progesterone relaxes ureteral muscle and the uterus compresses the ureters, more on the right.
Older men: prostatic enlargement (benign hyperplasia or cancer).
Women: pelvic tumors such as cervical cancer; any age: retroperitoneal fibrosis or neurogenic bladder.

notes.h: How back pressure injures the kidney
points: Pressure in the pelvis and tubules rises and opposes filtration, so GFR falls.
Filtration continues at a lower rate and filtrate leaks back into the interstitium.
High pressure compresses medullary vessels; the papillae lose blood flow and atrophy first, so concentrating ability fails early.
With time the cortex thins and scars, leaving a dilated pelvis surrounded by a thin rim of tissue.
Unilateral obstruction can stay silent for a long time because the other kidney keeps creatinine normal.
Bilateral obstruction (or bladder outlet block) causes postrenal acute kidney injury with oliguria or anuria.
After relief, postobstructive diuresis washes out retained urea, sodium, and water, and damaged tubules cannot concentrate; watch for dehydration and low potassium.
Calcium oxalate: the most common stone; hypercalciuria is the usual cause; also hyperoxaluria after ileal disease and ethylene glycol.
Calcium phosphate: forms in alkaline urine, as in distal renal tubular acidosis and primary hyperparathyroidism.
Struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate): urease-producing bacteria such as Proteus alkalinize urine; forms staghorn calculi.
Uric acid: forms in acidic urine; radiolucent on plain X-ray; seen in gout and tumor lysis.
Cystine: hexagonal crystals in cystinuria, often in children, can form staghorns.
A stone in the ureter causes waves of severe flank pain radiating to the groin, with hematuria and nausea.
Stones lodge at three narrow points: the ureteropelvic junction, where the ureter crosses the iliac vessels, and the ureterovesical junction (narrowest).
Complications: obstruction, hydronephrosis, and infection above the stone.
An infected obstructed kidney can turn into pyonephrosis and sepsis and needs urgent drainage.

charts.title: Kidney stones
rows: Distal renal tubular acidosis, primary hyperparathyroidism

tricks.label: Three tight spots
tricks.text: Picture the stone's trip: it sticks where the pelvis meets the ureter, where the ureter crosses the iliac vessels, and where it enters the bladder.

tricks.label: Alkaline builds phosphate
tricks.text: Phosphate stones (calcium phosphate and struvite) need alkaline urine; uric acid and cystine stones need acidic urine.

tricks.label: Papillae first
tricks.text: Obstruction hurts the inner medulla before the cortex, so the first lost function is the ability to concentrate urine.

highYield: Posterior urethral valves are the most common cause of bladder outlet obstruction in newborn boys.
Ureteropelvic junction obstruction is the most common cause of congenital hydronephrosis.
Unilateral obstruction may not raise creatinine; bilateral obstruction causes anuria.
Postobstructive diuresis follows relief of a long obstruction.
Calcium oxalate is the most common stone; hypercalciuria is the most common cause.
Uric acid stones do not show on plain X-ray.
Proteus urease makes struvite staghorn stones.
pitfalls: Calcium phosphate and calcium oxalate are both radiopaque; urine pH and crystal shape separate them.
Struvite and cystine can both form staghorns; struvite needs alkaline urine and infection, cystine shows hexagonal crystals.
A normal creatinine does not rule out obstruction of one kidney.
Hydronephrosis in pregnancy is usually physiologic and right-sided.
